analysis.one_liner: Toughens toy and children's product safety with mandatory independent testing, a strict lead ban, and bigger fines.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House floor vote; with 167 cosponsors it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee from September 2007 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a wave of recalls of lead-tainted toys, this bill would have required independent third-party testing of all children's products, banned any children's product containing more than 40 parts per million of lead, outlawed selling recalled products at retail, and made it easier for the Consumer Product Safety Commission to order recalls and public warnings. It would also have removed the cap on civil fines for safety violations and barred new federal rules from overriding state consumer lawsuits. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died there without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children, who would get safer toys and products: mandatory testing by independent labs, a near-total lead ban, tracking labels so buyers can identify a product's origin and batch, postage-paid registration cards so manufacturers can contact owners directly in a recall, and warning labels required in online ads. States and consumers suing over defective products would also benefit from new limits on federal preemption of state claims.

how_it_helps.text: Requires children's products to be tested by independent third-party labs, physically separate from and not controlled by the manufacturer, before they can be certified for sale [S2][S3].
Bans any children's product containing more than 40 parts per million of lead, with a temporary exception pathway for electronic devices [S2][S3].
Makes it unlawful to sell a product at retail that the seller knows is subject to a recall, and requires recall notices to be posted prominently on the seller's website [S2][S3].
Removes the $1,250,000 cap on civil penalties for related safety violations, letting the Commission set higher maximums, and eases the path to criminal prosecution [S2][S3].
Requires postage-paid product registration cards and permanent model/date markings so manufacturers can directly notify owners when a product is recalled [S3].
Bars new CPSC rules from preempting state-law damage suits unless expressly authorized, preserving consumers' ability to sue in state court [S2][S3].

Cuts from 30 days to 10 days the notice manufacturers get before the CPSC can publicly disclose hazard information, and increases agency funding from roughly $75.6 million in 2008 to $125 million by 2012 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Toy makers, children's product manufacturers, importers, and retailers, who would bear the cost of independent testing, lead-free reformulation, tracking labels and registration systems, and potentially much larger fines and recall liabilities.

drawbacks.text: Independent third-party testing, reformulation to meet the 40 ppm lead limit, and registration-card systems would raise manufacturing costs, costs that could be passed to consumers and that weigh most heavily on small manufacturers [S3].

The 40 parts per million lead threshold is stricter than the phase-in levels Congress later enacted in the Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act (which allowed higher limits before stepping down), so some products might have been pulled from the market faster than supply chains could adapt.
Removing the cap on civil penalties and shortening the notice period before public disclosure increases legal exposure and could pressure companies into costly over-recalls.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefits are substantial and the compliance costs, while real, are the kind the industry already largely accepted a year later when Congress passed similar testing and lead requirements. The bill's biggest design risk is the unusually strict 40 ppm lead limit, which could have disrupted supply chains, but its registration, tracking-label, and disclosure provisions directly address the chronic failure of recalls to reach families who already bought a dangerous product.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again; no hearing, no markup, no floor vote before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 27, 2007, by Rep. Rosa DeLauro and eight other House members during a period of high-profile toy recalls [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day; that was the final action of any kind in the bill's history [S5].
The bill attracted 167 cosponsors, 166 Democrats and 1 Republican, but that support never translated into committee action or a floor vote [S4].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Toy and children's product manufacturers and importers were better off: they avoided mandatory independent testing, the 40 ppm lead ban, uncapped civil fines, and easier state-court lawsuits for the remainder of the Congress. The CPSC also avoided the expanded recall authority and funding mandate.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.role: Sponsor; lead House advocate for stronger consumer product safety rules
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled eight original cosponsors, all focused on children's product safety after the 2007 toy recall wave

for.name: 167 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill, giving it broad House backing that never produced committee action

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on September 27, 2007, and took no further action — no hearing or markup — for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 166 of 167 cosponsors were Democrats, with a single Republican — and the bill died in a House committee without a vote, so the fight never reached the floor to be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to pay for independent lab testing, strip lead out of products at a 40 ppm limit, add tracking labels and registration cards, and face uncapped fines. Those costs are the direct flip side of the safety protections families would have gained.

Retailers would face new liability for knowingly selling recalled products, required website recall notices, and CPSC inspections extending to retail stores, but would benefit from registration cards that make recalls reach customers faster.
Mandatory third-party testing of every children's product would have created a large new market for accredited independent labs.
The bill would have expanded the agency's recall authority, raised its funding from about $75.6 million to $125 million by 2012, and made it easier to act with fewer than three members present.
